prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 800 words of John Snow's investigation of the 1854 cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London. The reader is a general reader with no medical background.

Do not use em dashes.

text:
In late August 1854, a terrible illness struck the crowded district of Soho in London. Within days, hundreds of people living near Broad Street were dying of cholera, a disease that causes violent vomiting and diarrhea and can kill a healthy adult in a day or two through sheer loss of fluid. Within about ten days, more than five hundred people had died. Many families fled. Shops closed. The streets, one observer wrote, fell strangely quiet.

At the time, almost nobody in authority knew what caused cholera. The dominant belief was the miasma theory: that disease spread through "bad air," foul smells rising from rotting waste and filth. It was a reasonable guess in a city that stank. London had no proper sewage system for most of its people. Cesspools beneath houses overflowed, and the River Thames served as both a drain and a source of drinking water.

John Snow, a physician living a few streets from Broad Street, doubted the theory. He was a careful, unusual man. He had become famous for pioneering the use of anaesthesia, and had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He did not drink alcohol, he was a vegetarian at a time when that was rare, and he trusted measurement over tradition. He had already published an argument in 1849 that cholera was carried in contaminated water, not in the air. His evidence was thin, and few people were persuaded.

His reasoning was simple. Cholera attacked the bowels first, not the lungs. If the poison were breathed in, he asked, why would the first symptoms appear in the gut? It made more sense that people swallowed something, and that whatever they swallowed multiplied inside the body and passed out again in waste. If that waste got into drinking water, the disease would spread.

When the Broad Street outbreak began, Snow saw a chance to test his idea on a small, well-defined population. He did what few doctors then did: he went door to door. He walked the streets, visited homes, and asked families where they got their water and who had fallen sick. He obtained the official list of deaths from the local registrar and began tracing each address.

Most households in the area drew their water from a public pump on Broad Street. As he mapped the deaths, Snow noticed that they clustered tightly around that pump. He drew the cases on a street map, marking each death with a bar. The bars piled up near the pump like a dark stain spreading outward. Maps showing disease clusters were not new, but Snow used his to make a clear argument.

The details mattered most, and Snow chased the exceptions. A workhouse nearby housed hundreds of people, yet very few of them died. He discovered it had its own well inside the building, so its residents never touched the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street also escaped almost untouched. The workers there were given free beer, and they were not in the habit of drinking from the pump. Meanwhile, deaths occurred far from Broad Street in a few cases, and Snow tracked these down as well. One was a widow living in Hampstead, miles away. Her son explained that she had once lived in Soho and loved the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle of it carried to her every day. She drank it, fell ill, and died. A niece who visited and drank from the same supply died too. Nobody else in her neighbourhood was sick.

Snow also examined a sample of the pump water under his microscope. He saw nothing conclusive. The tools of the day could not reveal the bacterium responsible, which would not be identified for decades. His case rested on patterns, not on proof of the cause itself.

On 7 September, Snow presented his findings to the local Board of Guardians. He asked them to remove the handle of the Broad Street pump, so nobody could draw water from it. The officials were skeptical, but they agreed. The handle was taken off the next day. The outbreak was already declining by then, since many residents had fled and the worst of the infection had passed, so critics later argued the removal made little difference. Snow himself acknowledged the numbers were falling. But the action still became a symbol of the whole story.

Later investigation supported his reasoning. A local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, who had originally been a skeptic, began his own inquiries and identified the likely source: a baby who had died of cholera at 40 Broad Street, whose soiled nappies were washed into a cesspool that leaked close to the well. The well, it turned out, had been poorly dug and lined, allowing contamination to seep in.

Official bodies still resisted Snow's conclusion. A committee investigating the outbreak concluded there was no reason to abandon the miasma theory. Snow died in 1858, aged forty-five, still not widely vindicated. Only later, as microbiology advanced and the cholera bacterium was identified, did his work gain recognition. Today he is regarded as one of the founders of epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. His lasting lesson is not just about a pump. It is that careful counting, honest attention to the exceptions, and the courage to follow evidence over habit can save lives.
